Widespread from the Himalayas to the Sundas in lowland forests

jasiuscharaxes.region: Southern Europe along the Mediterranean, North Africa, sub-Saharan Africa, western Asia
jasiuscharaxes.intro: The Two-tailed Pasha is the only Charaxes occurring in Europe and one of the largest butterflies of the Mediterranean. The wings have an orange band along the margins and two prominent hindwing tails; the underside is patterned like a mosaic. Adults love rotten fruit and never visit flowers, are extremely pugnacious, larvae feed on strawberry trees, and there are two generations a year.
highlights: Europe's only Charaxes and one of the largest Mediterranean butterflies
Orange marginal band, twin hindwing tails, mosaic-patterned underside
Males defend territories aggressively; their wing-clap is audible meters away

brenthisino.region: Europe across temperate Asia to Japan and Korea
brenthisino.intro: The Lesser Marbled Fritillary is a small leopard fritillary distributed across temperate Eurasia. The orange-brown upperside resembles the Pallas Fritillary but is darker; the underside is largely coffee-brown with white comma- or 'C'-shaped crescents, source of its name. Larvae feed on stinging nettle and meadowsweet from Europe across temperate Asia to Japan.
highlights: Underside marked with white comma- or 'C'-shaped crescents, source of the name
Upperside resembles the Pallas Fritillary but darker in tone
Larvae feed on nettle and meadowsweet, widespread across Eurasia

undosaeuthalia.region: Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Sichuan in China (China endemic)
undosaeuthalia.intro: The Wavy Euthalia is a Chinese-endemic Euthalia. Sexes look much alike, with grey-green-brown ground crossed by sharply outlined yellow-white spot bands arranged in a slightly wavy line. It inhabits low-mountain forests in Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, and Sichuan, with larvae feeding on Quercus glauca (Fagaceae); a common forest nymphalid in the Tianmu Mountains.
highlights: Endemic to China; grey-green wings crossed by wavy yellow-white spot bands
Sexes are similar; larvae feed on Quercus glauca (Fagaceae)
A common Euthalia in the low-mountain forests of the Tianmu Mountains

cyanecethosia.region: India to southern China (Yunnan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Sichuan) and Indochina
cyanecethosia.intro: The Plain Lacewing has reddish-brown male uppersides crossed by a diagonal white forewing band, with a deeply serrated wing margin and pronounced sexual dimorphism. Distributed from India to southern China and Indochina, it has spread to the Malay Peninsula and Singapore in recent years. Gregarious, larvae feed on passion vines and adults fly slowly along forest edges.
highlights: Serrated wing margin and a diagonal white forewing band, source of its name
Strong sexual dimorphism; larvae feed gregariously on passion vines
Recently expanded southward to the Malay Peninsula and Singapore

penthesileacet.region: Southeast Asia (Java, Timor, Sumba) and Northern Territory, Australia
penthesileacet.intro: The Tawny Lacewing is a brightly colored Cethosia with large orange patches edged in black and elongated white forewing spots. It inhabits monsoon forests and vine thickets from Southeast Asia to the Northern Territory of Australia, lives along streams, with larvae feeding exclusively on Adenia (Passifloraceae) vines—most often seen at the start of the dry season.
highlights: Large orange patches edged in black with elongated white forewing spots
Inhabits monsoon-forest streamsides; larvae feed on Adenia vines
Distributed from Southeast Asia to the Northern Territory of Australia

andromachaacr.region: Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, Australia, and Fiji
andromachaacr.intro: The Glasswing (Acraea andromacha) has nearly transparent forewings like glass and white hindwings with a wide black band inset with white spots and red dots—the 'star spots' giving it its name. Distributed from Indonesia through New Guinea to Australia and Fiji, larvae feed on passion vines, adults sequester toxins, and slow drifting flight protects them from most predators.
highlights: Glass-like translucent forewings; black hindwing band inset with star-like spots
Larvae sequester passion-vine toxins; adults drift slowly without fear
Distributed from Indonesia to Australia and Fiji along tropical forest edges

morganegreta.region: Mexico, Central America to northern South America
morganegreta.intro: Morgan's Greta is a close relative of the broader-banded Glasswing (Greta oto). The wing membrane between the dark veins is transparent like glass, with a thickened forewing apex. It inhabits humid rainforests from Mexico to northern South America, drifting close to the ground, the transparent wings and dark patterns blending into the surroundings—a textbook ithomiine mimicry model.
highlights: Glass-like wing membrane with crisp dark veins
Thickened forewing apex distinguishes it from Greta oto
Inhabits Neotropical rainforests; transparency hides it from predators

thyodamascyr.region: Himalayas, India, Indochina, southern/central/eastern China, Japan and Taiwan
thyodamascyr.intro: The Common Map (also called the Map Butterfly or Wallflower) has white or cream wings densely crossed by fine brown lines like a map. Widespread from the Himalayas through Southeast Asia to southern China and Japan, larvae feed on Ficus (Moraceae). It often perches on tall canopy or rock faces, holding its wings flat at rest, with slow flight.
highlights: Wings crossed by fine brown lines like a map—a textbook 'map butterfly'
Larvae feed on Ficus; often perches on tall canopy or rock faces
Wavy hindwing margins with short tails; rests with wings spread

issoriaacraea.region: Central, eastern, southern, and southwestern China, western Himalayas, Southeast Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines
issoriaacraea.intro: The Yellow Coster has yellow-brown wings ringed in a wide black border inset with grey-white spots; the wings are tough and translucent. Widespread from southern China through the Himalayas and Southeast Asia, larvae feed gregariously on ramie and other Urticaceae plants and accumulate toxins, while the slow drifting flight reduces predation.
highlights: Yellow-brown wings with wide black borders; tough, translucent wings
Larvae feed gregariously on ramie, a common pest of ramie plantations
Adults sequester toxins; their drifting flight evades most predators

terpsicoreacr.region: India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia to the Maldives, Myanmar; recently extended to Australia
terpsicoreacr.intro: The Tawny Coster has bright orange wings with black spots and white-dotted margins, with long tough wings. Widespread from India and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia in grasslands and shrub, in the past decade or so it has spread quickly eastward to Australia. Slow, drifting flight; the bright orange is a warning color, and most insect predators avoid it.
highlights: Bright orange wings with black spots and white-dotted margins, very conspicuous
Common in grassland and shrub; recently spread quickly to Australia
Orange warning color plus body toxins keep predators away

hypseacethosia.region: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, southern Thailand, Philippines
hypseacethosia.intro: The Malay Lacewing has crimson wings with black-and-white apical spots and deeply serrated margins—a vivid Cethosia of Southeast Asian rainforests. Distributed from the Malay Peninsula to the Sundas, larvae feed gregariously on Adenia (Passifloraceae) vines and accumulate toxins; slow flight, often gathering at forest-edge flowers.
highlights: Crimson wings with black-and-white apical spots and deeply serrated margins
A vivid lacewing of the Sundas rainforests; larvae feed gregariously on Adenia
Toxic body, slow flight, with bright color as a warning signal

lethevermayb.region: Himalayas, southern China to Indochina lowland and mid-elevation forests
lethevermayb.intro: The Banded Treebrown (Lethe verma) has smoky-brown wings; a wide diagonal white band like a jade belt crosses the forewing, while the hindwing has a row of marginal eyespots. It inhabits low- and mid-elevation forest shade, feeding on tree sap, rotten fruit, and damp ground; larvae feed on Phyllostachys and other bamboos. The sexes are similarly patterned.
highlights: A wide diagonal white band crosses the forewing like a jade belt
A row of yellow-ringed black eyespots along the hindwing margin
Feeds on sap and rotten fruit in shaded forest; larvae feed on bamboo

niceastibo.region: Himalayas, India, Nepal to southern and eastern China, Indochina
niceastibo.intro: The Glossy Sergeant (Athyma) is a velvety nymphalid; males have black-velvet wings with even rows of white spots set off by blue lines, and three short blue-white streaks in the cell. Distributed from the Himalayas to southern China and Indochinese mountain forests, it flies swiftly, often resting on low shrubs or damp ground with wings spread, and visits carnivore dung to draw minerals.
highlights: Velvety black wings with neat rows of white spots and blue line edging
Three blue-white streaks in the cell; females duller and greenish
Swift flight; rests with wings spread, visits dung for minerals

bisaltidedolesch.region: India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia to southern China, northern Australia
bisaltidedolesch.intro: The Autumn Leaf is named for its underside resembling a fallen leaf, with the midline acting as a leaf vein crossing both wings, while the upperside is orange-yellow with a dark forewing apex. Widespread from India through Southeast Asia to southern China and northern Australian rainforests, larvae feed on Acanthaceae plants. At rest with closed wings it perfectly mimics a dead leaf—a classic parallel evolution to the Indian Leafwing.
highlights: Orange-yellow upperside with dark forewing apex; underside mimics a dead leaf with veins
Larvae feed on Acanthaceae; adults love rotten fruit and tree sap
Famous parallel-evolution leaf mimic, paralleling Kallima

eginaacraea.region: Sub-Saharan Africa: from West and Central Africa to East and Southern Africa
eginaacraea.intro: The Wandering Donkey is a familiar large African Acraea with red-orange wings; the dark forewing apex is inset with orange-and-white spot rows, and the underside is sprinkled with white stars and black dots. Widespread along forest edges and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, larvae feed on Passifloraceae and accumulate toxins; slow flight is supported by warning colors.
highlights: Red-orange wings; black forewing apex inset with orange-white spot rows
Underside sprinkled with white stars and black dots—source of the Chinese 'white star' name
Widespread in Africa; larvae sequester passion-vine toxins as warning defense

eightyeight.region: Central America to central South America; type locality Guyana
eightyeight.intro: The 88 Butterfly is named for the concentric black lines on its hindwing underside that resemble the number 88—the type species of the genus Diaethria. Distributed from Central to central South America, larvae feed on Trema (Cannabaceae) and adults feed on rotten fruit and dung juice, often perching on leaves to display the iconic number pattern.
highlights: Hindwing underside black lines form the number 88, the source of the name
Upperside shows iridescent blue-green bands on black with red forewing bases
Larvae feed on Trema; adults feed on rotten fruit and dung juice
